translations.text: These are the names of the sons of Israel who entered Egypt with Jacob their father; each entered with his entire household.
Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah,
Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin,
Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher.
All the people descended from Jacob numbered seventy-five, and Joseph was in Egypt.
Joseph died, as did all his brothers and that entire generation.
The children of Israel grew and became vigorous; they multiplied and became very strong, for the land increased their numbers.
Another king arose who did not know Joseph.
He said to his people, “Look, the people of the children of Israel are great in strength and are becoming stronger than we are.
Now come, let us devise a plan against them, lest they multiply and, if war befalls us, join our enemies, fight against us, and leave this land.”
He appointed taskmasters over them to afflict them with labor. They built fortified cities for Pharaoh: Pithom, Rameses, and On, which is the City of the Sun.
The more they oppressed them, the more they multiplied and became very strong, and the Egyptians detested the children of Israel.
The Egyptians forcibly subjected the children of Israel to their rule.
They embittered their lives with hard labor in clay and brickmaking and with every kind of work in the fields—all the work in which they forced them to serve.
The king of the Egyptians spoke to the Hebrew midwives, one of whom was named Shiphrah and the other Puah.
He said, “When you assist the Hebrew women in childbirth and they are about to give birth, if the child is male, kill him; if female, keep her alive.”
But the midwives feared God and did not do as the king of the Egyptians had commanded them; they kept the male children alive.
The king of the Egyptians summoned the midwives and said to them, “Why have you done these things and kept the male children alive?”
The midwives said to Pharaoh, “The Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women, for they give birth before the midwives come to them.”
And they gave birth, and God dealt kindly with the midwives. The people multiplied greatly and became very strong.
Because the midwives feared God, they established households for themselves.
Pharaoh commanded all his people, saying, “Throw every male child born to the Hebrews into the river, but keep every female child alive.”
There was a man from the tribe of Levi who took a wife from among the daughters of Levi.
She conceived and gave birth to a male child. They saw that he was healthy and hid him for three months.
When they could no longer hide him, his mother took a reed basket, coated it with pitch, put the child in it, and placed it in a marsh by the riverbank.
His sister watched from a distance to see what would happen to him.
Pharaoh’s daughter went down to bathe in the river, and her maidservants walked along the river. Seeing the basket there among the reeds, she sent a maidservant to fetch it.
She opened it and saw the child, and the child was crying there in the basket. Pharaoh’s daughter had compassion on him and said, “This is one of the Hebrews’ children.”
His sister said to Pharaoh’s daughter, “Would you like me to call a Hebrew nurse for you, so that she can nurse the child for you?”
Pharaoh’s daughter said, “Go.” The girl went and called the child’s mother.
Pharaoh’s daughter said to her, “Take this child and nurse him for me, and I will pay you your wages.” The woman took the child and nursed him.
When the child grew strong, she brought him to Pharaoh’s daughter, and he became her adopted son. She named him Moses, saying, “I drew him out of the water.”
After many days, when Moses had grown up, he went out to his brothers, the Israelites. Looking at their suffering, he saw an Egyptian man beating a Hebrew, one of his brothers, one of the Israelites.
He looked this way and that and saw no one. He struck down the Egyptian and hid him under the sand.
He went out on the second day and saw two Hebrew men fighting with each other. He said to the man who was doing wrong, “Why are you striking your companion?”
The man said, “Who appointed you ruler and judge over us? Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?” Moses was struck with fear and said, “So the matter has become known.”
Pharaoh heard about the matter and sought to kill Moses. Moses fled from Pharaoh’s presence and settled in the land of Midian. When he came to the land of Midian, he sat beside a well.
The priest of the Midianites had seven daughters who tended their father’s flocks. They had come to draw water, and they filled the troughs to water their father’s flocks.
Other shepherds came and drove them away. Moses rose and rescued them, drew water for them, and watered their flocks.
They came to Reuel their father, and he said to them, “Why have you come back while it is still daylight today?”
They said, “An Egyptian man rescued us from the shepherds, drew water, and watered our flocks.”
He said to his daughters, “And where is he? Why did you leave the man behind? Now call him so that he may eat bread.”
Moses settled with the man, and he gave his daughter Zipporah to Moses as his wife.
His wife conceived and bore a son, and Moses named him Gershom, saying, “For I am a stranger in a foreign land.”
After many days, the king of the Egyptians died. The Israelites were suffering because of their labor and cried out, and their cry because of their labor rose before God.
God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
God looked upon the Israelites and made himself known to them.
Moses tended the flocks of Jethro his father-in-law, the priest of the Midianites. He led the flocks into the wilderness and came to the mountain of God, to Horeb.
The angel of the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire from the midst of a bush. He saw that the bush was burning with fire, but the bush was not being consumed.
Moses said, “I will go over and see this great sight: why is the bush not being consumed?”
When the Lord saw that he was approaching to look, the Lord called to him from the midst of the bush, saying, “Moses, Moses!” He said, “What is it?”
He said, “Do not come near here. Take your shoes off your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground.”
He said to him, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Moses turned his face away, for he was afraid to look upon God.
The Lord said to Moses, “I have indeed seen the suffering of my people who are in Egypt, and I have heard their cry because of their taskmasters, for I know their sorrows.”

And I have come down to rescue them from the hands of the Egyptians, to bring them out of that land and lead them to a good and spacious land, a land flowing with milk and honey, the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, Girgashites, and Jebusites.
And now, look, the cry of the children of Israel has reached me, and I have seen the oppression with which the Egyptians oppress them.
And now come, I will send you to Pharaoh, king of the Egyptians, and you will bring my people, the children of Israel, out of the land of the Egyptians.
And Moses said to God, “Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh, king of the Egyptians, and bring the children of Israel out of the land of the Egyptians?”
He said, “I will be with you, and this will be the sign to you that I sent you to bring my people out of Egypt: you will worship God on this mountain.”
And Moses said to God, “Suppose I go to the children of Israel and say to them, ‘The God of your fathers has sent me to you,’ and they ask me, ‘What is his name?’ What shall I say to them?”
And God said to Moses, “I am God, THE ONE WHO IS.” And he said, “This is what you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘THE ONE WHO IS has sent me to you.’”

And God said again to Moses, “This is what you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘The Lord, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.’ This is my name forever, and this is how I am to be remembered from generation to generation.”

Now go, gather the council of elders of the children of Israel, and say to them, “The Lord, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, appeared to me and said, ‘I have surely attended to you and to everything that has happened to you in Egypt.’”

And I say, “I will bring you out of the land of suffering under the Egyptians into the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Girgashites, Hivites, and Jebusites, a land flowing with milk and honey.”

And they will listen to your voice. You and the council of elders of the children of Israel shall go to Pharaoh, king of the Egyptians, and say to him, “The Lord, the God of the Hebrews, calls us to himself. Now let us go a three days’ journey into the wilderness, so that we may sacrifice to the Lord our God.”
And I know that the king of the Egyptians will not let you go except under a mighty hand.
And I will stretch out my hand and strike Egypt with all my wonders that I will perform among them, and afterward he will release you.
And I will give my people favor in the sight of the Egyptians, and when you leave, you shall not leave empty-handed.

Instead, each woman shall ask her neighbor and the woman who shares her house for vessels of gold, vessels of silver, and clothing. You shall adorn your sons and daughters with them, and you shall plunder the Egyptians.
Moses answered and said, “If they do not believe me and do not listen to my voice, because they say, ‘God has not appeared to you,’ what shall I say to them?”
The Lord said to him, “What is that in your hand?” And he said, “A staff.”
And he said, “Throw it on the ground.” And he threw it on the ground, and it became a snake, and Moses fled from it.
And the Lord said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand and grasp it by the tail.” And he stretched out his hand and grasped it by the tail, and it became a staff in his hand.
“So that they may believe you, that the Lord, the God of their fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has appeared to you.”
The Lord said to him again, “Put your hand inside your robe.” And he put his hand inside his robe and took it out, and his hand had become leprous, like snow.
And he said, “Put your hand inside your robe.” And he put his hand inside his robe and took it out, and it was restored once again to the color of his own flesh.
“If they do not believe you and do not heed the message of the first sign, they will believe you because of the message of this second sign.”

And if they do not believe these two signs and do not listen to your voice, take some water from the river and pour it onto dry ground. The water you take from the river will become blood on the dry ground.
Moses said to the Lord, “I beg you, Lord, I am not capable, neither yesterday nor the day before, nor since you began speaking with your servant, for I am weak-voiced and slow of speech.”
The Lord said to Moses, “Who gave a human being a mouth? Who made the deaf and the mute, the sighted and the blind? Was it not I, God?
Now go, and I will open your mouth and teach you what you must say.”
He said, “I beg you, Lord, choose someone else who is capable to send.”

The Lord became fiercely angry with Moses and said, “Is not Aaron the Levite your brother there? I know that he will certainly speak with you. Look, he will come out to meet you, and when he sees you, he will rejoice in his heart.
You will speak with him and put my words in his mouth. I will open your mouth and his mouth and teach you both what to do.
He will speak to the people on your behalf. He will be your mouth, and you will stand in the place of God for him.
Take in your hand this staff that turned into a snake, with which you will perform the signs.”
Moses went back to Jethro, his father-in-law, and said to him, “Let me return to my brothers in Egypt and see whether they are still alive.” Jethro said to Moses, “Go in peace.”
After those many days, the king of the Egyptians died. The Lord said to Moses in Midian, “Go back to Egypt, for all the men who sought your life have died.”
Moses took his wife and his children, put them on pack animals, and returned to Egypt. Moses took the staff from God in his hand.

The Lord said to Moses, “When you go and return to Egypt, see that you perform before Pharaoh all the signs that I have placed in your hands. But I will harden his heart, and he will not let the people go.”
You will say to Pharaoh, “This is what the Lord says: Israel is my firstborn son.
I told you, ‘Let my people go so that they may worship me.’ But if you refuse to let them go, I myself will kill your firstborn son.”
On the journey, at a lodging place, an angel of the Lord met him and sought to kill him.
Zipporah took a flint and circumcised her son’s foreskin. Falling at his feet, she said, “Look, the blood from my child’s circumcision has stopped.”
The angel departed from him because she said, “The blood from my child’s circumcision has stopped.”
The Lord said to Aaron, “Go into the wilderness to meet Moses.” He went and met him at the mountain of God and kissed him.
Moses told Aaron all the words of the Lord, who had sent him, and all the signs that he had commanded him to perform.
Moses and Aaron went and gathered all the elders of the Israelites.
Aaron spoke all the words that the Lord had spoken to Moses and performed the signs before the people.
The people believed and rejoiced because God had visited the Israelites and had seen their suffering. The people bowed down and worshiped.
Then Moses and Aaron went in before Pharaoh and said to him, “This is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says: Let my people go so that they may hold a festival for me in the wilderness.”
Pharaoh said, “Who is he, that I should obey his voice and let the Israelites go? I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go.”
They said to him, “The God of the Hebrews has called us to himself. Now let us go three days’ journey into the wilderness to sacrifice to the Lord our God, lest death or slaughter befall us.”
The king of the Egyptians said to them, “Why do you, Moses and Aaron, keep the people from their work? Go, each of you, to your own work.”
Pharaoh said, “Look, the people in the land are increasing greatly. Now let us not give them rest from their work.”
That day Pharaoh gave orders to the people’s taskmasters and their scribes, saying:
Do not continue giving the people straw for making bricks as you did yesterday and the day before. Let them go and gather straw for themselves.
“Impose on them the same quota of bricks that they used to make each day. Do not reduce it at all, because they are idle. That is why they cry out and say, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to our God.’”
Let the work weigh heavily on the men, so that they attend to it and pay no attention to empty words.
The people's taskmasters and their scribes pressed them, speaking to the people and saying, “This is what Pharaoh says: I will no longer give you straw.
Go yourselves and gather straw wherever you can find it, for nothing at all will be deducted from your quota.”
The people scattered throughout the whole land of Egypt to gather reeds for straw.
The taskmasters pressed them, saying, “Complete your work according to the daily quota, just as when straw was given to you.”

The scribes of the people of Israel, whom Pharaoh's overseers had placed over them, were beaten. The overseers said, “Why have you not completed your quota of bricks as you did yesterday and the day before, and also today?”
The scribes of the Israelites went in and lodged a complaint before Pharaoh, saying, “Why do you treat your servants this way?
No straw is given to your servants, yet they order us to make bricks. Look, your servants are being beaten, and you are oppressing your own people.”
He said to them, “You are idle! You are lazy! That is why you say, ‘Let us go and offer sacrifices to our God.’
Now go and work. No one will give you straw, but you must deliver the full quota of bricks.”
The scribes of the Israelites saw that they were in distress and said, “No one reduces our daily quota of bricks.”
When they came out from Pharaoh’s presence, they met Moses and Aaron, who were coming toward them.
They said to them, “May God see and judge you, because you have made our smell repulsive to Pharaoh and his servants, putting a sword into his hands to kill us.”
Moses returned to the Lord and said, “Lord, why have you afflicted your people, and why did you send me?
Ever since I went to Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has afflicted the people, and you have not rescued your people at all.”
The Lord said to Moses, “Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh. With a mighty hand he will release them, and with an uplifted arm he will drive them out of his land.”
God spoke to Moses and said to him, “I am the Lord.
I appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. I am their God, but I did not reveal my name, the Lord, to them.
I established my covenant with them to give them the land of the Canaanites, where they lived as foreigners.
I have heard the groaning of the Israelites, whom the Egyptians have enslaved, and I have remembered my covenant.

Go, speak to the Israelites and say, ‘I am the Lord. I will bring you out from under the oppression of the Egyptians, rescue you from slavery to them, and save you with an uplifted arm and great acts of judgment.
I will take you as my people, and I will be your God. You will know that I am the Lord your God, who brings you out from under the oppression of the Egyptians.
I will bring you into the land that I raised my hand to give to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and I will give it to you as an inheritance, for I am the Lord.’”
Moses spoke this way to the Israelites, but they did not listen to him because of their discouragement and their harsh labor.
The Lord spoke to Moses and said:
“Go in and speak to Pharaoh, king of the Egyptians, so that he will let the Israelites leave the land of the Egyptians.”
Moses spoke before the Lord and said, “Look, the Israelites have not listened to me. How will Pharaoh listen to me, when I am not a capable speaker?”
The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron and gave them instructions concerning the Israelites and Pharaoh, king of Egypt, to bring the Israelites out of the land of Egypt.
These are the heads of their ancestral houses: the sons of Reuben, Israel’s firstborn, were Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi. This is the tribe of Reuben.
The sons of Simeon were Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, who was of Phoenician descent. These are the clans of the sons of Simeon.
These are the names of the sons of Levi according to their clans: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. Levi lived 137 years.
The sons of Gershon were Libni and Shimei, with their ancestral houses.
The sons of Kohath were Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. Kohath lived 133 years.
The sons of Merari were Mahli and Mushi. These are the ancestral houses of Levi according to their clans.
Amram took Jochebed, the daughter of his father’s brother, as his wife. She bore him Aaron, Moses, and Miriam their sister. Amram lived 137 years.
The sons of Izhar were Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri.
The sons of Uzziel were Mishael, Elzaphan, and Zithri.
Aaron took Elisheba, the daughter of Amminadab and sister of Nahshon, as his wife. She bore him Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.
The sons of Korah were Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph. These are the clans of Korah.
Eleazar, Aaron’s son, took one of Putiel’s daughters as his wife, and she bore him Phinehas. These are the leaders of the ancestral houses of the Levites according to their clans.
These are Aaron and Moses, to whom God said, “Bring the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt with their armies.”
These are the ones who argued with Pharaoh, king of Egypt, to bring the children of Israel out of Egypt—this Moses and Aaron.
On the day when the Lord spoke to Moses in the land of Egypt,
the Lord spoke to Moses and said, “I am the Lord. Tell Pharaoh, king of Egypt, everything that I tell you.”
Moses said before the Lord, “Look, my voice is weak. How will Pharaoh listen to me?”
The Lord said to Moses, “See, I have made you a god to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother will be your prophet.
You shall tell him everything that I command you, and Aaron your brother shall tell Pharaoh to release the children of Israel from his land.
“I will harden Pharaoh’s heart and multiply my signs and wonders in the land of the Egyptians.”
Pharaoh will not listen to you, and I will lay my hand on Egypt and bring my people, the children of Israel, out of the land of Egypt with my power and with great acts of vengeance.
The Egyptians will know that I am the Lord, and I will stretch out my hand against Egypt and bring the children of Israel out from among them.”
Moses and Aaron did just as the Lord commanded them; so they did.
Moses was eighty years old, and Aaron was eighty-three years old when they spoke to Pharaoh.
The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron and said,

“If Pharaoh speaks to you and says, ‘Give us a sign or a wonder,’ you shall say to Aaron your brother, ‘Take your staff and throw it on the ground before Pharaoh and his servants, and it will become a dragon.’”
Moses and Aaron went in before Pharaoh and did as the Lord had commanded them. Aaron threw down his staff before Pharaoh and his servants, and it became a dragon.
Pharaoh called the wise men of Egypt and the sorcerers, and the magicians of Egypt did the same through their sorcery.
Each one threw down his staff, and they became serpents, but Aaron’s staff swallowed their staffs.
Pharaoh’s heart hardened, and he did not listen to them, just as the Lord had said.
The Lord said to Moses, “Pharaoh’s heart has become stubborn, so that he will not let the people go.”
“Go to Pharaoh in the morning. He will be going out to the water. Stand facing him on the riverbank, and take in your hand the staff that turned into a snake.”
“Say to him, ‘The Lord, the God of the Hebrews, sent me to you, saying, “Let my people go, so that they may worship me in the wilderness.” But you have not listened to me up to now.’”
“‘This is what the Lord says: “By this you will know that I am the Lord. Look, with this staff in my hand I will strike the water of this river, and it will turn to blood.”’”
“‘“The fish in this river will die, the river will stink, and the Egyptians will be unable to drink water from it.”’”

The Lord said to Moses, “Tell Aaron, ‘Take your staff and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt, over their rivers, their lakes, their pools, and their bodies of collected water, and they will become blood.’” And there was blood throughout the land of the Egyptians, in wooden and stone containers.
Moses and Aaron did as the Lord had commanded them. He raised his staff and struck the water of the river before Pharaoh and his servants, and turned all the water of the river into blood.
The fish in the river died, and the river stank. The Egyptians could not drink water from the river, and there was blood throughout the land of the Egyptians.
The wise men of Egypt did the same through their magic. Pharaoh’s heart hardened, and he did not listen to them, just as the Lord had said.
Pharaoh turned and went into his house, and did not take even this to heart.
All the Egyptians dug around the river for drinking water, because they could not drink water from the river.
Seven days passed after the Lord struck the river.
The Lord said to Moses, “Go in to Pharaoh and say to him, ‘This is what the Lord says: “Let my people go, so that they may worship me.”’”
“‘“But if you refuse to let them go, I will strike your entire territory with frogs.”’”

“‘“The river will teem with frogs. They will come up and enter your houses, the inner chambers of your bedrooms, and your beds, and the houses of your servants and your people, and your ovens and your dough.”’”
“‘“The frogs will come up onto you, your people, and your servants.”’”
The Lord said to Moses, “Tell Aaron your brother, ‘Stretch out the staff in your hand over the river, the canals, and the pools, and bring frogs up over the land of the Egyptians.’”
Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of the Egyptians and brought up frogs. The frogs came up and covered the land of the Egyptians.
The wise men of Egypt did the same through their magic and brought up frogs in the land of the Egyptians.
Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said, “Pray to the Lord, and let him remove the frogs from me and my people. Then I will let the people go, and they may sacrifice to the Lord.”

Moses said to Pharaoh, “Set a time for me: when shall I pray for you, your servants, and your people, to destroy the frogs on you and your people and in your houses, so that they remain only in the river?”
He said, “Tomorrow.” And Moses said, “It will be as you have said, so that you may know that there is no other besides the Lord our God.”
“The frogs will be removed from you, your houses, your servants, and your people. They will remain only in the river.”
Moses and Aaron went out from Pharaoh, and Moses cried out to the Lord about the time appointed for the frogs, as he had agreed with Pharaoh.
The Lord did as Moses had said, and the frogs died in the houses, the courtyards, and the fields.
They gathered them into heaps, and the land stank.
When Pharaoh saw that there was relief, his heart grew hard, and he did not listen to them, just as the Lord had said.
The Lord said to Moses, “Tell Aaron, ‘Stretch out your staff with your hand and strike the dust of the ground, and it will become gnats on people and animals throughout the land of Egypt.’”
They did so. Aaron stretched out his staff with his hand and struck the dust of the ground, and gnats appeared on people and animals and throughout all the dust of the land of Egypt.
The magicians likewise tried to bring forth gnats by their magic, but they could not. The gnats were on people and animals.
The magicians said to Pharaoh, “This is the finger of God.” But Pharaoh’s heart grew hard, and he did not listen to them, just as the Lord had said.

The Lord said to Moses, “Rise early in the morning and stand before Pharaoh. He will be going out to the water, and you shall say to him, ‘This is what the Lord says: Let my people go, so that they may worship me.

But if you are unwilling to let my people go, I will send biting flies upon you, your servants, your people, and your houses. The Egyptians’ houses will be filled with biting flies, as will the ground on which they stand.

On that day I will make the land of Goshen, where my people are, stand apart in a wonderful way: there will be no biting flies there, so that you may know that I am the Lord, the Lord of all the earth.
I will make a distinction between my people and your people. Tomorrow this sign will come upon the land.’”
The Lord did so, and great numbers of biting flies came into Pharaoh’s houses, into his servants’ houses, and throughout the land of Egypt. The land was devastated by the biting flies.
Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said, “Go and sacrifice to the Lord your God here in this land.”

Moses said, “We cannot do that, because we would be sacrificing to the Lord our God what the Egyptians consider detestable. If we sacrifice what the Egyptians consider detestable before their eyes, they will stone us.
Instead, we will go a three-day journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the Lord our God, just as the Lord told us.”
Pharaoh said, “I will let you go, and you may sacrifice to the Lord your God in the wilderness. Only do not go far away. Now pray to the Lord for me.”

Moses said, “I will leave you and pray to God, and tomorrow the biting flies will depart from Pharaoh, his servants, and his people. But Pharaoh must not deceive us again by refusing to let the people go to sacrifice to the Lord.”
Moses left Pharaoh and stood in prayer before God.
The Lord did as Moses had said and removed the biting flies from Pharaoh, his servants, and his people. Not a single one remained.
But Pharaoh hardened his heart this time too and was unwilling to let the people go.
The Lord said to Moses, “Go to Pharaoh and say to him, ‘This is what the Lord, the God of the Hebrews, says: Let my people go, so that they may worship me.
But if you are unwilling to let my people go and still hold them back,
the hand of the Lord will come upon your livestock in the fields—upon the horses, donkeys, camels, cattle, and sheep—with a very severe, deadly plague.’”
“I will work wonders among the livestock of the Egyptians and among the livestock of Israel, and not a single one belonging to any of the Israelites will perish.”
God set a time, saying, “Tomorrow the Lord will do this thing upon the land.”
The Lord did this the next day, and all the Egyptians’ livestock died, but not one of the Israelites’ animals perished.
When Pharaoh saw that not one of the Israelites’ animals had perished, his heart grew hard, and he did not let the people go.
The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron and said, “Take handfuls of ashes from a furnace, and let Moses scatter them toward heaven before Pharaoh and his servants.”
It will become dust throughout the land of Egypt, and it will cause sores with erupting blisters on people and animals throughout the land of Egypt.
They took ashes from the furnace before Pharaoh, and Moses scattered them toward heaven. They became sores with erupting blisters on people and animals.
The magicians could not stand before Moses because of the sores, for the sores afflicted the magicians too, and all the land of Egypt.
The Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he did not listen to them, just as the Lord had told Moses.
The Lord said to Moses, “Rise early in the morning, stand before Pharaoh, and say to him, ‘This is what the Lord, the God of the Hebrews, says: Let my people go, so that they may worship me.’”
For at this time I will send all my plagues upon your heart, upon your servants, and upon your people, so that you may know that there is no one like me in all the earth.
For I will stretch out my hand and strike you and your people with death, and you will be wiped out from the earth.
But you were spared for this reason: that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth.
Are you still exalting yourself over my people to oppress them?
Look, tomorrow at this time I will send down very severe hail, such as has never occurred in Egypt from the day it was founded until today.
Now hurry to gather your livestock and everything you have in the fields, for the hail will fall on every person and animal found in the fields that has not come indoors, and will kill them.
Every one of Pharaoh’s servants who feared the word of the Lord brought his servants and livestock indoors.
But whoever did not take the Lord’s words to heart left his servants and livestock in the fields.

The Lord said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand toward heaven, and there will be hail over all the land of the Egyptians—over people and livestock and over every plant in the fields of the land of the Egyptians.”
Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and the Lord sent thunder and hail. Fire ran across the land, and the Lord rained hail upon the land of Egypt.
There was hail, with fire blazing amid the hail. The hail was very severe, such as had never occurred in all the land of Egypt since a nation had existed there.
Throughout the land of Egypt, the hail struck everything in the fields, from people to animals. The hail struck every plant in the fields and shattered every tree in the fields.
But in the land of Goshen, where the children of Israel were, there was no hail.
Pharaoh sent for Moses and Aaron and said to them, “This time I have sinned. The Lord is righteous, and I and my people are wicked.”
“Pray to the Lord for me, and let God’s thunder, the hail, and the fire cease. I will let you go, and you will no longer have to stay.”

Moses said to him, “As soon as I leave the city, I will stretch out my hands to God. The thunder will cease, and there will be no more hail or rain, so that you may know that the earth belongs to the Lord.”
“But I know that you and your servants do not yet fear the Lord God.”
The flax and barley were struck down, for the barley was in ear and the flax had produced seed.
But the wheat and spelt were not struck down, because they ripened late.
Moses left Pharaoh and went outside the city. He stretched out his hand to the Lord, and the thunder and hail ceased, and rain no longer fell upon the earth.
When Pharaoh saw that the rain, hail, and thunder had ceased, he sinned again and hardened his own heart and the hearts of his servants.
Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he did not let the children of Israel go, just as the Lord had said through Moses.
The Lord spoke to Moses and said, “Go to Pharaoh, for I have hardened his heart and the hearts of his servants, so that my signs may come upon them in succession.
So that you may tell your children and your children’s children how I made sport of the Egyptians, and about the signs I performed among them, and you may know that I am the Lord.”

Moses and Aaron went before Pharaoh and said to him, “This is what the Lord, the God of the Hebrews, says: ‘How long will you refuse to humble yourself before me? Let my people go so that they may worship me.
But if you refuse to let my people go, look, at this same time tomorrow I will bring a terrible swarm of locusts over all your territory.
They will cover the whole surface of the land, and you will not be able to see the ground. They will eat everything left to you by the hail, and they will eat every tree growing for you in the land.

Your houses, the houses of all your servants, and the houses throughout the land of Egypt will be filled with them—something neither your fathers nor their ancestors have ever seen, from the day they came into existence on earth until today.’” Then he turned away and left Pharaoh.
Pharaoh’s servants said to him, “How long will this be an obstacle to us? Let the people go so that they may worship the Lord their God. Are you willing to recognize that Egypt is ruined?”
Moses and Aaron were brought back to Pharaoh, and he said to them, “Go and worship the Lord your God. But who exactly will go?”
Moses said, “We will go with our young and our old, with our sons and daughters. We will go with our cattle and sheep, for it is a festival of the Lord our God.”
He said to them, “May the Lord be with you like that, since I am letting you go! Am I to let your possessions go too? Look, evil is among you!
Not so! Only the men may go and worship God, for that is what you were asking for.” And they were driven out of Pharaoh’s presence.

The Lord said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand over the land of Egypt, and let locusts come up over the land of Egypt and eat every plant in the land and all the fruit of the trees that the hail left.”
Moses raised his hand toward heaven, and the Lord brought a south wind upon the land all that day and all that night. When morning came, the south wind carried the locusts.
He brought them over the whole land of Egypt and made them settle throughout all the territory of Egypt. Before that there had never been such locusts, and afterward there were never any like them.

They covered the whole surface of the land, and the land was ruined. They ate every plant in the land and all the fruit of the trees that remained after the hail. Nothing green remained on the trees or among any of the plants of the field throughout the whole land of Egypt.
Pharaoh hurried to summon Moses and Aaron and said, “I have sinned before the Lord your God and against you.”
“Now forgive my offenses this once more, and plead with the Lord your God to remove these locusts from me.”
Moses left Pharaoh and stood in prayer before God.
The Lord turned the wind into a strong wind from the sea, which carried away the locusts and cast them into the Red Sea. Not a single locust remained in the whole land of Egypt.
The Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he did not let the Israelites go.
The Lord said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand toward heaven, and let there be darkness over the land of Egypt—darkness that can be felt.”
Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and there was darkness, gloom, and deep shadow over the whole land of Egypt for three days.
No one could see his brother for three days, and no one rose from his bed for three days. But all the Israelites had light in all their dwellings.
Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said to them, “Go and worship the Lord your God, but leave your cattle and sheep here. The rest of your households may go with you.”
And Moses said, “Yes, you must also give us burnt offerings and sacrifices, which we will offer to the Lord our God.”

“Our livestock must also go with us, and we will not leave even one hoof behind, because we will take from them to worship the Lord our God. We do not know what we will offer to the Lord our God until we arrive there.”
And the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he was unwilling to let them go.
And Pharaoh said, “Get away from me! Watch yourself! Do not see my face again, for on the day you appear before me, you will die.”
And Moses said, “You have said it. I will not appear before your face again.”
And the Lord said to Moses, “I will bring one more plague upon Pharaoh and upon Egypt, and then he will release you from here. When he releases you, he will drive you out of here altogether.”
“Now speak privately in the hearing of the people, and let each man ask his companion, and each woman her neighbor, for gold vessels, silver vessels, and clothing.”

And the Lord gave his people favor in the sight of the Egyptians, and they gave them things for adornment. And the man Moses was very highly esteemed before the Egyptians, before Pharaoh, before all his servants, and in the eyes of the people.
And Moses said, “This is what the Lord says: ‘At midnight I will enter the midst of Egypt.’”

“‘And I will kill every firstborn in the land of the Egyptians, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sits on his throne, to the firstborn of the slave woman who is at the millstones, and to the firstborn of all the livestock.’”
“‘And there will be a great cry throughout the land of the Egyptians, such as has never occurred and will never occur again.’”

“‘But among all the children of Israel, not even one dog will growl with its tongue, at either a person or an animal, so that you may know how great are the wonders the Lord will perform between the Egyptians and Israel.’”

“And all these servants of yours will come down to me and bow before me, saying, ‘Leave, you and all your people whom you lead.’ And then I will leave.” And Moses went out from Pharaoh, full of anger.
And the Lord said to Moses, “Pharaoh will not listen to you, so that I may multiply my signs and wonders in the land of the Egyptians.”

And Moses and Aaron performed all these signs and wonders in the land of the Egyptians before Pharaoh. And the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he would not release the children of Israel from the land of the Egyptians.
And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron in the land of the Egyptians, saying:
“This month shall be the beginning of the months for you; it shall be the first of the months of the year for you.”

“Speak to the whole congregation of the children of Israel and say: ‘On the tenth day of this month, each shall take a sheep for himself, according to their family households, one sheep for each household.’”

“‘If there are too few in the household to consume the sheep, he shall take his neighbor and his companion along with him, according to the number of people. Each person shall be counted toward the sheep according to how much he can eat.’”
“‘Your sheep shall be a perfect male, a year old, without blemish. You shall take it from the sheep or the goats.’”
“‘You shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month, and the whole assembly of the congregation of the children of Israel shall slaughter it toward evening.’”
“‘They shall take some of the blood and put it on the two doorposts and on the lintel of the houses in which they eat it.’”
“‘They shall eat the meat that night, roasted over fire, and they shall eat unleavened bread with [?].’”
“‘You shall not eat any of it raw, nor [?] boiled in water, but roasted over fire, its head together with its legs and its entrails.’”
“‘You shall leave none of it until morning, and you shall not break a bone of it. Whatever remains of it until morning, you shall burn with fire.’”
And this is how you shall eat it: with your belts around your waists, your shoes on your feet, and your staffs in your hands. Eat it in haste, for it is the Lord’s Passover.

And I will pass through the whole land of Egypt on this night and strike down every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from humans to livestock. I will execute judgment against all the gods of Egypt, for I am the Lord.
And the blood shall be a sign for you on the houses where you are. I will see the blood and save you, and no destructive blow shall fall upon you when I strike the land of Egypt.
And this day shall be a memorial for you, and you shall celebrate it as a feast to the Lord. Throughout your generations, you shall celebrate it as an everlasting ordinance.

For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread. From the very first day, you shall remove leaven from your houses. Anyone who eats anything leavened from the first day through the seventh day shall be cut off from Israel.

And the first day shall be called holy, and the seventh day shall be consecrated as holy for you. You shall do no work on it, except what must be prepared for each person; only that may be done for you.
And you shall keep this commandment of mine, for on this day I brought your forces out of the land of Egypt. You shall observe this day throughout your generations as an everlasting ordinance.
Beginning on the fourteenth day of the first month, in the evening, you shall eat unleavened bread until the evening of the twenty-first day of the month.
For seven days no leaven shall be found in your houses. Anyone who eats anything leavened shall be cut off from the people of Israel, whether a foreign resident or a native of the land.
No one shall eat anything leavened. In all your dwellings you shall eat unleavened bread.
And Moses called together all the elders of the children of Israel and said to them, “Go and take sheep for yourselves according to your families, and slaughter them for the Passover.

And take a bunch of hyssop, dip it in the blood that is at the doorway, and sprinkle the lintel and the two doorposts with the blood that is at the doorway. But none of you shall go out through the door of your house until morning.

And the Lord will pass through to strike the Egyptians. He will see the blood on the lintel and on the two doorposts, and the Lord will pass over the doorway and will not allow the destroyer to enter your houses to strike you.
And you shall keep these words as an ordinance for yourself and your children forever.
And when you enter the land that the Lord will give you, as he has said, you shall keep this observance.
And when your children say to you, ‘What does this observance mean to you?’

you shall say to them, ‘This is the Lord’s Passover sacrifice, when he protected the houses of the children of Israel in Egypt while striking the Egyptians, and saved our houses.’” And the people bowed down and worshiped.
And the children of Israel went and did as the Lord had commanded Moses and Aaron; that is what they did.

And at midnight the Lord struck down every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sat on his throne, to the firstborn of the captive who was in the dungeon, and every firstborn of the livestock.
And Pharaoh rose during the night, he and all his servants and all the Egyptians. There was a great cry throughout the whole land of Egypt, for there was no house without someone dead in it.
And Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron during the night and said to them, “Get up and leave my people, both you and the children of Israel. Go and worship the Lord your God, as you said.
Take your cattle and your sheep and go, as you said. But bless me also.”
And the Egyptians pressed the people to send them out of the land in haste, for they said, “We are all dying!”
And the people took their dough before it was leavened, with their lumps of dough wrapped in their cloths on their shoulders.
The Israelites did as Moses had commanded them and asked the Egyptians for gold vessels, silver vessels, and clothing.
The Lord gave his people favor in the sight of the Egyptians, and they lent these things to them. Thus they plundered the Egyptians.
The Israelites set out from Rameses for Succoth, six hundred thousand men on foot, besides the other members of their households.
A great multitude also went with them, along with cattle, sheep, and very many livestock.

They baked the dough they had brought out of Egypt into unleavened cakes, because it had not risen. The Egyptians had driven them out, and they could not stay, nor had they prepared provisions for their journey.
The time the Israelites and their fathers lived in the land of the Egyptians and in the land of the Canaanites was four hundred and thirty years.
At the end of four hundred and thirty years, on that very day, all the hosts of the Lord went out of the land of the Egyptians.
It was a night of vigil for the Lord to bring them out of the land of the Egyptians. That night is to be a vigil for the Lord for all the Israelites throughout their generations.
The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron and said, “This is the law of the Passover: no foreigner shall eat of it.
You shall circumcise every servant belonging to anyone who has been bought with silver, and then he may eat of it.
A temporary resident or a hired worker shall not eat of it.
It shall be eaten in one house. You shall not take any of the meat outside the house, and you shall not break any of its bones.
The whole congregation of the Israelites shall observe it.

If a foreigner comes to live among you and wishes to observe the Passover of the Lord, you shall circumcise every male child of his. Then he may come forward to observe it, and he shall be like a native of the land. No uncircumcised person shall eat of it.
One and the same law shall apply to the native and to the foreigner who comes to live among you.”
All the Israelites did just as the Lord had commanded Moses and Aaron.
On that very day, the Lord brought the Israelites out of the land of the Egyptians with their hosts.
The Lord spoke to Moses and said:
Consecrate to me every firstborn, the first offspring that opens any womb among the Israelites, whether human or animal, for it is mine.
Moses said to the people, “Remember this day on which you came out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, for the Lord brought you out of here with a mighty hand. You shall not eat anything leavened.
For today you are going out, in the month of the early crops.

When the Lord your God brings you into the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Hivites, Jebusites, Perizzites, and Girgashites, which he swore to your fathers to give you, a land flowing with milk and honey, you shall perform this observance in this month.
You shall eat unleavened bread for seven days, and on the seventh day there shall be a feast to the Lord.
You shall eat unleavened bread for seven days. Nothing leavened shall be seen among you, and there shall be no leaven anywhere within your borders.
On that day you shall tell your son, saying, ‘This is because of what the Lord God did for me when I came out of Egypt.’
It shall be a sign for you on your hand and a reminder before your eyes, so that the laws of the Lord may be in your mouth, for the Lord brought you out of Egypt with a mighty hand.
You shall keep this law at its appointed times, from year to year.
When the Lord your God brings you into the land of the Canaanites, as he swore to you and your fathers, and gives it to you,
You shall set apart for the Lord every male that opens the womb, and every firstborn from your herds and livestock that you possess. The males shall be holy to the Lord.
You shall exchange every firstborn donkey for a sheep, and if you do not exchange it, you shall redeem it. You shall redeem every firstborn among your sons.
If your son later asks you, ‘What is this?’ you shall tell him, ‘With a mighty hand the Lord brought us out of the land of the Egyptians, out of the house of slavery.’

When Pharaoh stubbornly refused to release us, the Lord killed every firstborn in the land of the Egyptians, from the firstborn of humans to the firstborn of livestock. Therefore I offer to the Lord every male that opens the womb, and I will redeem every firstborn among my sons.
It shall be a sign on your hand and a fixed mark before your eyes, because with a mighty hand the Lord brought us out of Egypt.
When Pharaoh released the people, God did not lead them through the land of the Philistines by the short road, for God said, ‘The people might lose courage when they see war and return to Egypt.’
God led the people around by the road through the wilderness toward the Red Sea. The children of Israel came out of the land of the Egyptians in the fifth generation.
Moses took Joseph’s bones with him, because Joseph had made the children of Israel swear an oath, saying, ‘When the Lord surely visits you, you shall carry my bones up from here with you.’
The children of Israel set out from Succoth and camped at Etham, beside the wilderness.
God led them by day with a pillar of cloud to show them the road, and by night with a pillar of fire to give them light, so that they could travel by night and by day.
The pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night never departed from before all the people.
And the Lord spoke to Moses and said:
Speak to the children of Israel, and let them turn back and camp opposite the encampment, between Migdol and the sea, facing Baal-zephon. You shall camp opposite them, by the seashore.
Pharaoh will say of the children of Israel, ‘They are wandering in the land, for the wilderness has hemmed them in.’
I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, and he will pursue them. I will be glorified through Pharaoh and all his forces, and all the Egyptians will know that I am the Lord. And they did so.

The king of the Egyptians was told that the people had fled, and the hearts of Pharaoh and his servants turned against the people. They said, ‘What have we done, releasing the children of Israel so that they no longer serve us?’
Pharaoh prepared his chariots and took all his people with him.
He took six hundred chosen chariots and all the horses of the Egyptians, with armed men over all of them.
The Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh, king of the Egyptians, and he pursued the children of Israel. The children of Israel were going out with uplifted hands.
And the Egyptians pursued them and found them camped beside the sea—all Pharaoh’s horses and chariots, his horsemen and his army—in front of the resting place, opposite Baal-zephon.
Pharaoh drew near, and the children of Israel lifted their eyes and saw that the Egyptians had camped behind them. They were very afraid, and the children of Israel cried out to the Lord.
They said to Moses, ‘Was it because there were no graves in the land of the Egyptians that you brought us out to kill us here in the wilderness? What have you done to us, bringing us out of Egypt?’
‘Is this not what we told you in the land of the Egyptians: “Leave us alone so that we may serve the Egyptians”? It was better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in this wilderness.’

And Moses said to the people, “Take courage, stand firm, and see the salvation from the Lord that he will bring you today. For you will never again see the Egyptians as you see them today, for all time.”
“The Lord will fight for you, and you must remain silent.”
And the Lord said to Moses, “Why do you cry out to me? Speak to the children of Israel, and let them move on.”
“Take your staff, stretch out your hand over the sea, and divide it, and let the children of Israel enter the midst of the sea on dry ground.”
And behold, I will harden the heart of Pharaoh and of all the Egyptians, and they will go in after them. And I will be glorified through Pharaoh and all his army, his chariots and his horses.
“And all the Egyptians will know that I am the Lord when I am glorified through Pharaoh, his chariots, and his horses.”
And the angel of God, who was going before the camp of the children of Israel, moved and went behind them. And the pillar of cloud moved from before them and stood behind them.
And it came between the camp of the Egyptians and the camp of the Israelites. There was darkness and mist, and the night passed, and they did not mingle with one another throughout the night.
And Moses stretched out his hand over the sea and drove the sea back by the force of a south wind all night. He made the sea dry land, and the water was divided.
And the children of Israel entered the midst of the sea on dry ground, and the water became a wall on their right and on their left.
The Egyptians took courage and went in after them—all Pharaoh’s horses, his chariots, and his horsemen—into the midst of the sea.
And during the morning watch, the Lord looked upon the camp of the Egyptians through the pillar of fire and cloud, and threw the camp of the Egyptians into confusion.
And he bound the wheels of their chariots and made them move with difficulty. The Egyptians said, “Let us flee from Israel, for the Lord is fighting for them against us Egyptians.”
And the Lord said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand over the sea, and let the water join together again and cover the Egyptians, their chariots, and their horsemen.”
And Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and toward morning the water returned to its place. The Egyptians fled before the water, and the Lord hurled the Egyptians into the midst of the sea.
And the returning waters covered the chariots, the horsemen, and all Pharaoh’s army that had gone into the sea after them. Not even one of them remained.
But the children of Israel walked on dry ground in the midst of the sea, and the water was a wall on their right and on their left.
And on that day the Lord saved Israel from the hands of the Egyptians, and Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the seashore.
And Israel saw the mighty hand that the Lord had used against the Egyptians. The people feared the Lord and believed in God and in Moses his servant.
Then Moses and the children of Israel sang this song of praise to God, saying, “Let us praise the Lord, for he has been glorified in glory; he has cast the horses and their riders into the sea.”
“The Lord is my helper and refuge, and he has become my salvation. He is my God, and I will glorify him, the God of my father, and I will exalt him.”
“The Lord crushes wars; the Lord is his name.”
“He cast Pharaoh’s chariots and his forces into the sea. The chosen horsemen and the armed men were drowned in the Red Sea.”
“The depths covered them; they sank into the abyss like a stone.”
“Your right hand, Lord, is glorified in power; your right hand, Lord, crushed the enemy.”
“And in the greatness of your glory you shattered your adversaries. You sent out your wrath, and it consumed them like reeds.”
“And by the blast of your anger the waters were divided. The waters froze like a wall; the waves froze in the midst of the sea.”
The enemy said, “I will pursue and overtake them. I will divide the plunder and satisfy myself with them. I will destroy them with my sword; my hand will rule over them.”
You sent your wind, and the sea covered them; they sank like lead in the mighty waters.
Who is like you among the gods, Lord? Who is like you, glorified among the holy ones, wondrous in glory, working signs?
You stretched out your right hand, and the earth swallowed them.
In righteousness you led this people of yours whom you redeemed; with your strength you comforted them in your holy dwelling place.
The nations heard and grew angry, and anguish seized the inhabitants of Canaan.
Then the judges of Edom were distressed, and trembling seized the rulers of the Moabites. All the inhabitants of Canaan melted away.
May terror and fear fall upon them. By the greatness of your arm, let them become like stone until your people pass through, Lord, until this people of yours whom you acquired pass through.
You will bring them in and plant them on the mountain of your inheritance, in the place you prepared for your dwelling, Lord—the sanctuary, Lord, which your hands prepared.
The Lord is king forever and ever, and beyond.
For Pharaoh’s horses went into the sea with his chariots and horsemen, and the Lord brought the waters of the sea upon them. But the Israelites walked on dry land in the midst of the sea.
Miriam the prophetess, Aaron’s sister, took the tambourine in her hand, and all the women went out after her with tambourines and dancing.
Miriam led and said, “Let us praise the Lord, for he is gloriously glorified; he has thrown the horses and their riders into the sea.”
Moses led the Israelites away from the Red Sea and brought them into the wilderness of Shur. They traveled for three days in that wilderness and found no water to drink.
They came to Marah, but they could not drink the water at Marah because it was bitter. Therefore he named that place Bitterness.
The people grumbled against Moses and said, “What shall we drink?”

Moses cried out to the Lord, and the Lord showed him a piece of wood. He threw it into the water, and the water became sweet. There he established statutes and judgments for him, and there he tested him.

And he said, “If you listen carefully to the voice of the Lord your God, do what is pleasing in his sight, heed his commandments, and keep all his ordinances, I will not bring upon you any of the diseases that I brought upon the Egyptians, for I am the Lord who heals you.”
They came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they camped there beside the water.

They departed from Elim, and the whole community of the Israelites came to the wilderness of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month after their departure from the land of Egypt.
The whole community of the Israelites grumbled against Moses and Aaron there in the wilderness.

The Israelites said to them, “It would have been better if we had died by the blows of the Lord in the land of Egypt, when we sat beside the pots of meat and ate bread until we were full, rather than for you to bring us out into this wilderness to kill this whole community with hunger.”
The Lord said to Moses, “Look, I will rain bread from heaven for you. My people shall go out and gather each day’s portion, so that I may test them to see whether they will follow my law or not.”
“On the sixth day they shall prepare what they bring in, and it shall be twice as much as they gather each day.”
Moses and Aaron said to the whole community of the Israelites, “In the evening you will know that the Lord brought you out of the land of Egypt.”
“And in the morning you will see the glory of the Lord, because he has heard your grumbling against God. But who are we, that you grumble against us?”

Moses said, “When the Lord gives you meat to eat in the evening and bread in the morning until you are full, it is because the Lord has heard the grumbling that you direct against us. For who are we? Your grumbling is not against us, but against God.”
Moses said to Aaron, “Say to the whole community of the Israelites, ‘Come before the Lord, for he has heard your grumbling.’”
While Aaron was speaking to the whole congregation of the Israelites, they turned toward the wilderness, and there the glory of the Lord appeared in a cloud.
And the Lord spoke to Moses and said:

I have heard the grumbling of the Israelites. Now speak to them and say, “In the evening you will eat meat, and in the morning you will have your fill of bread, and you will know that I am the Lord your God.”
In the evening, quail came up and covered the camp, and in the morning dew fell around the camp.
And behold, on the surface of the wilderness there was something small like coriander, white like frost on the ground.
When the Israelites saw it, they said to one another, “What is this?” For they did not know what it was. Moses said to them, “This is the bread that the Lord has given you to eat.”

This is what the Lord has commanded: “Gather some of it, each as much as he needs, a measure per person, according to the number of people you have. Each of you is to gather it for those in his tent.”
The Israelites did so and gathered it, some much and some little.
They measured it with the measure, and whoever had gathered much had nothing extra, while whoever had gathered little had no shortage. Each had gathered as much as he needed.
Moses said to them, “Let no one leave any of it until morning.”
But they did not listen to Moses. Some left part of it until morning, and it swarmed with worms and rotted. Moses was angry with them.
And they gathered it morning by morning, each according to what he needed, and when the sun grew hot, it melted.
On the sixth day they gathered twice the provisions, two measures for each person. All the leaders of the congregation came and reported this to Moses.

Moses said to them, “This is what the Lord has said: Tomorrow is a Sabbath rest, holy to the Lord. Whatever you are going to bake, bake, and whatever you are going to boil, boil. Leave all that remains in containers until morning.”
They left some of it until morning, as Moses had commanded them, and it did not rot, nor were there worms in it.
And Moses said, “Eat this today, for today is a Sabbath to the Lord. Today you will not find it in the field.”
Gather it for six days, but on the seventh day, the Sabbath, there will be none.
On the seventh day, some of the people went out to gather it, but they found none.
The Lord said to Moses, “How long will you refuse to obey my commandments and laws?”
See, the Lord has given you this Sabbath day. Therefore, on the sixth day he has given you bread for two days. Each of you must stay in your home, and no one is to leave his place on the seventh day.
The people rested on the seventh day.
The Israelites named it Manna. It was like coriander seed, white, and its taste was like honeycomb.

Moses said, “This is what the Lord has commanded: Put a full measure of this manna into a container and keep it throughout your generations, so that you may see the bread you ate here in the wilderness at the time when the Lord brought us out of the land of the Egyptians.”
Moses said to Aaron, “Take a golden jar, put a full measure of manna into it, and place it before God to be kept throughout your generations.”
As the Lord had commanded Moses, Aaron placed it before the Testimony for safekeeping.
The Israelites ate manna for forty years, until they came to an inhabited land. They ate manna until they reached the territory of the Phoenicians.
The measure was one tenth of three seahs.
The whole congregation of the Israelites set out from the wilderness of Sin, moving by their camps at the Lord’s command, and camped at Rephidim. There was no water for the people to drink.
The people complained against Moses and said, “Give us water to drink.” Moses said to them, “Why do you complain against me, and why do you put the Lord to the test?”
The people were thirsty for water there, and they complained against Moses, saying, “Why did you bring us out of Egypt to kill us, our children, and our livestock with thirst?”
Moses cried out to the Lord and said, “What shall I do with these people? A little more, and they will stone me.”
The Lord said to Moses, “Go ahead of the people and take some of the elders of the people with you. Take in your hand the staff with which you struck the river, and go.
I will arrive before you and stand there on the rock at Horeb. Strike the rock, and water will come out of it, and the people will drink.” Moses did so before the children of Israel.
He named that place Testing and Complaining, because the children of Israel complained and because they tested the Lord, saying, “Is the Lord among us or not?”
Amalek came and fought against Israel at Rephidim.
Moses said to Joshua, “Choose strong men for yourself, and go out and fight against Amalek tomorrow. I will go and stand on the top of the hill with the staff of God in my hand.”
Joshua did as Moses told him and went into battle against Amalek. Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill.
And whenever Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed, and whenever he lowered his hands, Amalek prevailed.

Moses’ hands grew heavy, so they took a stone and placed it beneath him, and he sat on it. Aaron and Hur supported his hands, one on this side and the other on that side, and Moses’ hands remained steady until sunset.
Joshua struck down Amalek and all his army with the sword.
The Lord said to Moses, “Write this in a book as a memorial and tell it in Joshua’s hearing, for I will utterly erase the memory of Amalek from the earth beneath heaven.”
Moses built an altar to the Lord and named it “The Lord Is My Refuge.”
He said, “For by the Lord’s hidden hand, the Lord wages war against Amalek from generation to generation.”
And Jethro, the priest of Midian, Moses’ father-in-law, heard everything that the Lord had done for Moses and for Israel, his people, and that the Lord had brought Israel out of Egypt.
Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, took Zipporah, Moses’ wife, after Moses had sent her away,
and her two sons. One was named Gershom, for Moses said, “I was a stranger in a foreign land.”
The second was named Eliezer, for he said, “The God of my father is my helper, and he rescued me from Pharaoh’s hands.”
Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, came with Moses’ sons and wife to Moses in the wilderness, where he was staying at the mountain of God.
Moses was informed, and they said, “Your father-in-law Jethro is coming to you, with your wife and your two sons.”
Moses went out to meet his father-in-law, bowed to the ground before him, and kissed him. They greeted one another in peace, and he brought them into the tent.
Moses told his father-in-law everything the Lord had done to Pharaoh and the Egyptians for Israel’s sake, all the hardships they had experienced on the journey, and how the Lord had rescued them.
Jethro was amazed at all the good things the Lord had done for them and that he had rescued them from the hands of the Egyptians and from Pharaoh’s hands.
And Jethro said, “Blessed is the Lord, who saved them from the hands of the Egyptians and from Pharaoh’s hand, for he delivered the people from under the hand of the Egyptians.”
“Now I know that the Lord is greater than all the gods, because they acted oppressively against these people.”
Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, brought burnt offerings and sacrifices to God. Moses, Aaron, and all the elders of Israel went to eat bread with Moses’ father-in-law before the Lord.
The next day, Moses sat down to judge the people, and all the people stood around Moses from morning until evening.
Jethro saw everything Moses was doing for the people and said, “What is this that you are doing for the people? Why do you sit alone while all the people stand around you from morning until evening?”
And Moses said to his father-in-law, “For the people come to me to seek judgment from God.
Whenever they have a dispute, they come to me, and I decide between one person and another and make God's commands and his laws known to them.”
And Moses' father-in-law said to him, “What you are doing is not right.
You and all the people with you are suffering unbearable hardship. This task is too heavy for you; you cannot do it alone.
But now listen to me, and I will give you advice, and God will be with you. Represent the people before God, and bring their cases to God.
Instruct them in God's commands and his laws, and show them the paths they should follow and the deeds they should do.

And select for yourself from all the people capable men who worship God, men firm in righteousness who hate arrogance, and appoint them over the people as leaders of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens.
Let them judge the people at all times. Let them bring every major case to you, but judge the minor cases themselves. They will lighten your burden and be your helpers.
If you do this, God will strengthen you, and you will be able to endure, and all these people will go to their own places in peace.”
And Moses listened to his father-in-law and did everything he had told him.
And Moses chose capable men from all Israel and appointed them over the people as leaders of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens.
And they judged the people at all times. They brought the major cases to Moses, but judged every minor case themselves.
And Moses sent his father-in-law on his way, and he went to his own land.
In the third month after the Israelites came out of the land of the Egyptians, on that very day they came to the wilderness of Sinai.
They set out from Rephidim and came to the wilderness of Sinai and camped there in the wilderness. And Israel camped there opposite the mountain.
And Moses went up to the mountain of God, and God called to him from the mountain and said, “This is what you shall say to the house of Jacob and tell the children of Israel:
‘You yourselves have seen all that I did to the Egyptians, and how I carried you as though on an eagle's wings and brought you to myself.
And now, if you truly listen to my voice and keep my covenant, you will be my own people among all the nations, for the whole earth is mine.
And you will be a kingdom and a priesthood and a holy nation for me.’ These are the words you shall speak to the children of Israel.”
Moses came and called the elders of the people and set before them all these words that God had commanded him.
The people answered together and said, “We will do everything God has said and obey.” And Moses brought the people's words to God.

And the Lord said to Moses, “Behold, I will come to you in a pillar of cloud, so that the people may hear when I speak with you and may believe you forever.” And Moses reported the people’s words to the Lord.
And the Lord said to Moses, “Go down, give the people solemn instructions, and consecrate them today and tomorrow, and let them wash their clothes.
And let them be ready for the third day, for on the third day the Lord will descend upon Mount Sinai in the sight of all the people.
And set boundaries for the people all around and say, ‘Take care not to go up the mountain or approach it, for anyone who approaches the mountain shall be put to death.

No hand shall touch him, for he shall be stoned with stones and pierced with arrows. Whether animal or human, he shall not live.’ But when the sounds and the trumpet and the cloud depart from the mountain, they shall go up the mountain.”
And Moses went down from the mountain to the people and consecrated them, and they washed their clothes.
And he said to the people, “Be ready for three days; do not have sexual relations with women.”

On the morning of the third day there were thunderclaps and flashes of lightning and a thick, misty cloud over Mount Sinai. The trumpet sounded very loudly, and all the people in the camp were terrified.
Moses brought the people out of the camp to meet God and stationed them around the foot of Mount Sinai.
Mount Sinai was entirely covered in smoke, because God had descended upon it in fire. Its smoke rose like the smoke of a furnace, and all the people were greatly terrified.
For the sounds of the trumpet continued and grew very loud. Moses spoke, and God answered him with a voice.
The Lord descended upon Mount Sinai, to the top of the mountain. The Lord called Moses to the top of the mountain, and Moses went up there.
And God spoke to Moses and said, “Go down and warn the people, lest they approach to look at God and many of them perish.”
“The priests who approach God must also sanctify themselves, lest the Lord destroy some of them.”
Moses said to God, “The people cannot go up Mount Sinai, because you yourself instructed us, saying, ‘Set the mountain apart and sanctify it.’”
The Lord said to him, “Go down, and come back up here, you and Aaron with you. But the priests and the people must not attempt to come up to God, lest the Lord destroy some of them.”
Moses went down to the people and spoke to them.
The Lord spoke all these words, saying:
“I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of the Egyptians, out of the house of slavery.
You shall have no other gods besides me.
You shall not make idols for yourself in the likeness of anything in heaven above, on the earth below, or in the waters beneath the earth.

You shall not bow down to them or worship them, for I am the Lord your God, a jealous God, who visits the sins of the fathers upon their children to the third and fourth generations of those who hate me.
And I show mercy to a thousand generations of those who love me and who keep my commandments.
You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain, for the Lord will not acquit anyone who takes his name in vain.
Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.
For six days you shall labor and do all your work.

On the seventh day there is a Sabbath to the Lord your God. On it you shall not do any work—you, your son, your daughter, your male servant, your female servant, your ox, your donkey, any of your livestock, your resident alien, or the foreigner staying with you.
For in six days the Lord God made heaven and earth and the sea and everything in them, and he rested on the seventh day. Therefore the Lord blessed the seventh day and made it holy.
Honor your father and your mother, so that it may go well with you and you may live long in the good land that the Lord your God will give you.
You shall not murder.
You shall not commit adultery.
You shall not steal.
You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor.

You shall not covet your neighbor’s house or his field. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, his male slave, his female slave, his ox, his donkey, any of his livestock, or anything that belongs to your neighbor.
All the people saw the thunder, the flashes, the sound of the trumpet, and the mountain smoking. All the people were struck with fear, drew back, and stood at a distance.
They said to Moses, “You speak to us, and we will listen. But do not let God speak to us, lest we die.”
And Moses said to them, “Take courage, for God has come to you to test you, so that the fear of him may be in you, so that you do not sin.”
The people stood at a distance, and Moses entered the dark cloud where God was.
The Lord said to Moses, “This is what you shall say to the house of Jacob and tell the children of Israel: ‘You yourselves have seen that I spoke to you from heaven.'
You shall not make gods of gold or gods of silver for yourselves.

You shall make an altar of earth for me and offer on it your burnt offerings and your peace offerings, your sheep and your cattle. In every place where I cause my name to be proclaimed, I will come to you and bless you.
But if you make an altar of stones for me, do not build it with hewn stones, for you have brought your tool against it, and it is defiled.
You shall not go up to my altar by steps, so that your private parts are not exposed over it.
These are the laws that you shall set before them.
If you buy a Hebrew slave, he shall serve you for six years, and in the seventh year he shall go free without payment.
If he entered alone, he shall leave alone. If he entered with a wife, his wife shall leave with him.
But if his master gives him a wife and she bears him sons and daughters, the wife and children shall belong to his master, and he shall leave alone.
But if the slave declares, “I love my master, my wife, and my children, and I will not go free,”
his master shall bring him before God’s court. Then he shall bring him to the doorpost and pierce his ear with an awl, and he shall serve him forever.
If someone sells his daughter into slavery, she shall not leave as female slaves leave.
If she does not please her master, to whom she was pledged, he shall have her redeemed. But he has no authority to sell her to a foreign people, because he has dishonored her.
But if he pledges her to his son, he shall treat her according to the laws for daughters.
If he takes another wife besides her, he shall not withhold her food, her clothing, or marital relations from her.
If he does not provide these three things for her, she shall leave freely, without payment.
If someone strikes another person and that person dies, he too shall be put to death.
But if it was not intentional, and God delivered the person into his hands, he shall be given a place where the killer may flee.
But if someone plans to kill his neighbor treacherously and flees, you shall take him even from my altar and put him to death.
Whoever strikes his father or his mother shall be put to death.
Whoever kidnaps one of the children of Israel and sells him, and he is found in his possession, shall be put to death.
Whoever reviles his father or his mother shall be put to death.
If two men quarrel and one of them strikes the other with a stone or a fist, and he does not die but takes to his bed,
if the man gets up and walks outside with a staff, the one who struck him shall be free of guilt, but shall compensate him for his lost time and his medical treatment.
If someone strikes his male or female slave with a rod, and the slave dies at his hand, vengeance shall be exacted through judgment.
But if he survives a day or two, vengeance shall not be sought, for they were bought with his own money.
If two men fight and strike a pregnant woman, and her embryo comes out unformed, he shall pay half the damages, whatever the woman's husband imposes on him, and shall pay at his request.
But if it is formed, he shall give life for life,
eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot,
burn for burn, wound for wound, blow for blow.
If someone strikes the eye of his male slave or the eye of his female slave and blinds it, he shall set them free in compensation for their eye.
And if he knocks out the tooth of his male slave or the tooth of his female slave, he shall set them free in compensation for their tooth.
If a bull gores a man or a woman and they die, the bull shall be stoned, and its meat shall not be eaten, but the bull's owner shall be free of guilt.

But if the bull was accustomed to goring before, and its owner had been warned but had not removed it, and it kills a man or a woman, the bull shall be stoned, and the bull's owner shall also be put to death.
But if a ransom is imposed on him, he shall pay a ransom for his life, according to the full amount imposed on him.
And if it gores a son or a daughter, they shall deal with him according to the same rule.
But if the bull gores a male slave or a female slave, he shall give their owner thirty double staters of silver, and the bull shall be stoned.
If someone opens a pit or digs a well and does not cover it, and an ox or a donkey falls into it,
the owner of the pit shall pay compensation in silver and give it to the animal's owner, and the carcass shall belong to him.
If someone's bull gores his neighbor's bull and it dies, they shall sell the living bull and divide its price, and they shall also divide the dead bull.
But if the bull was already known to gore, and its owner had been warned but had not removed it, he shall pay a bull for the bull, and the dead animal shall belong to him.
